David Livingstone
DAY-vid LIV-ing-stun
proper noun
David from the Hebrew Dawid, “beloved,” the name of Israel’s king; Livingstone a Scottish surname; he styled himself in his journals simply a missionary and a servant of Christ.

Biblical Definition

David Livingstone (1813–1873) was a Scottish missionary and explorer of Africa, a tireless foe of the slave trade, whose name passed into proverb through the greeting “Dr. Livingstone, I presume.” Born to poverty and set to the cotton mills as a boy, he taught himself by candlelight, trained in medicine and theology, and went out under the London Missionary Society to southern Africa. Finding the interior closed and the gospel hindered by the Arab and Portuguese slave traffic, he gave himself to opening the continent, that the highways of commerce and Christianity might break the chains of what he called “this open sore of the world.” He crossed Africa from coast to coast, charted the great river and the falls, and roused the conscience of Britain against the trade in men. Though his converts were few and his methods later questioned, his deeper aim never wavered: to bring light to the dark places of the earth (Psa 74:20) and to make a way for the messengers of Christ. He died on his knees in a hut at Ilala, his heart buried in the soil of the Africa he loved, his body carried home to Westminster. He held the gospel to be the only cure for the cruelty he witnessed, and his exposure of the slave trade helped end it. He stands as a giant among the laborers of the Great Commission.

Webster 1828 Definition

A Scottish missionary-explorer of Africa and enemy of the slave trade, whose journeys opened the interior to the gospel.

expand to see more

DAVID LIVINGSTONE, a Scottish missionary and explorer (1813–1873) sent to Africa by the London Missionary Society.

A former mill-boy, he trained in medicine and divinity and gave his life to the African interior.

He labored to abolish the Arab and Portuguese slave trade, which he called the open sore of the world.

He crossed the continent from coast to coast and made known its rivers, peoples, and need of Christ.

He died on his knees at Ilala; his heart was buried in Africa and his body in Westminster Abbey.

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

Modern Corruption

Livingstone’s legacy is now commonly recast by colonial-guilt revisionism as a herald of empire, with his lifelong war on slavery obscured.

expand to see more

The reigning revisionism files Livingstone among the architects of colonial conquest, an opener of Africa for European exploitation. This inverts the truth. Livingstone’s whole burden was to destroy the slave trade that was depopulating the continent, and he spent himself exposing the caravans of chained men and women that he met upon the road. He longed for legitimate commerce precisely to undercut the trade in human flesh, and he went unarmed for the gospel’s sake. To brand the man who pleaded “open thy mouth for the dumb” as an agent of oppression is to silence one of slavery’s greatest foes in the name of the very justice he served.

The lesson to recover is that the gospel is the true emancipator, and that those who carried it were often the foremost enemies of the world’s great cruelties. Livingstone’s explorations were not ends in themselves but a clearing of the way that the light of Christ might shine into the habitations of cruelty (Psa 74:20). A Reformed reckoning will own his failures as a husband and a strategist, yet honor the providence that used his weakness to rouse a nation’s conscience and to advance the kingdom of God in a darkened land.

Hebrew Roots

The “beloved” of his name went to the beloved lost of Africa as a servant of the King after God’s own heart.

expand to see more

David — Hebrew Dawid, “beloved,” the name of Israel’s shepherd-king.

Livingstone — a Scottish surname; a living stone built upon the chief corner stone (1Pe 2:5).

His own word for slavery was “the open sore of the world,” a wound he gave his life to heal.

The verb that ruled him was to go — ever further into the dark interior.

“Explorer” he was, but the territory he most sought to open was a way for the gospel.

Usage

"David Livingstone crossed an unmapped continent that the gospel might one day follow his trail."

"The slave caravans David Livingstone met upon the road haunted him to the end of his days."

"When at last he was found by Stanley, David Livingstone would not leave the work he had begun."
